title: Stress hormone response · FKBP5
summary: FKBP5 helps control how the body turns off its stress hormone response. At rs1360780, the T copy is linked to a stronger cortisol response that takes longer to settle. In people with major stress early in life, T is also linked to a modest rise in depressive episodes and stress symptoms. The link is weak or absent without that exposure. This is an interaction with life experience, not a fixed risk.

interpretations.TT: Two T copies occur in about 10% of people. Group studies link this type to a stronger cortisol response that takes longer to settle. Mainly after serious stress early in life, it is also linked to a modest rise in repeated depressive episodes. This is one small factor, and most people with TT never have these conditions. Support, life events, and many genes matter much more.
interpretations.CT: One T and one C copy give a middle stress hormone response on average. Any rise in stress-related symptoms is small and appears mainly after serious life adversity. This DNA change is one minor factor among hundreds of genetic and life influences.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, the most common genotype. Group studies find typical HPA-axis feedback and no elevated association with stress-related symptoms at this locus. This says nothing about overall susceptibility to stress or mood difficulties, which depend on many other genetic and life factors.

title: Social response · OXTR
summary: OXTR makes the receptor for oxytocin, a hormone involved in social bonds. Small studies link the G copy at rs53576 to slightly higher self-reported empathy on average. They link AA to a somewhat stronger stress response. Other studies did not find the same results, and any effect is small. This is an early research clue, not a measure of personality.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele. In some small studies this genotype was associated on average with slightly lower self-reported empathy scores and a somewhat larger physiological stress response. Other studies found no difference, and the effect, where seen, is small. Social skills and empathy are shaped overwhelmingly by experience and many other genes.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G allele. Group differences reported for this variant are small and inconsistently replicated, and heterozygotes generally fall in the middle of an already-overlapping range. Nothing about day-to-day social behaviour can be read from this genotype.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele. A few studies associated this genotype with higher average empathy scores and calmer stress responses, but replication has been mixed and the effect, if real, is small. This is one preliminary data point, not a measure of social ability.

title: Novelty seeking & attention · DRD4
summary: DRD4 makes a dopamine receptor long studied in attention traits and novelty seeking. The often discussed 7-repeat change cannot be read by common DNA arrays. This report uses the promoter change rs1800955, also called -521C/T. A review linked C to slightly higher novelty scores, but later and larger studies weakened the link. This result is preliminary.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele. In early studies and one meta-analysis this genotype was associated on average with slightly lower novelty-seeking scores than C carriers. The association has not held up consistently in larger samples, and personality traits like novelty seeking are highly polygenic and strongly shaped by environment.
interpretations.CT: One C and one T copy have only small, mixed links to approach-related personality traits. This promoter change is also an imperfect stand-in for the DRD4 repeat changes studied in attention research. Common DNA arrays cannot read those repeats.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies reduce DRD4 promoter activity in lab tests. A 2008 review linked C to modestly higher novelty scores on average. Later, larger studies found little or no effect. This is a small, uncertain factor among the many genes and experiences that shape temperament.

title: COMT types differ in how they work.
summary: COMT helps break down dopamine, a brain signal. Its Val and Met forms differ in enzyme activity. A study of 497 college students linked this gene region to some personality scores in women. That does not show how well someone handles sudden stress or pain.

interpretations.GG: Your file shows two G copies, which code for Val. Val is the higher-activity form of this enzyme compared with Met. This does not make GG a test of calmness or better performance under stress.
interpretations.AG: Your file shows one G (Val) and one A (Met) copy. These forms differ in enzyme activity. That does not place your anxiety halfway between GG and AA; a protein difference is not a personality score.
interpretations.AA: Your file shows two A copies, which code for Met. Met is the lower-activity form of this enzyme compared with Val. Lower enzyme activity does not by itself show your brain's dopamine level or mean you are more anxious.

title: Bipolar · CACNA1C
summary: CACNA1C makes part of a calcium channel that is active in nerve cells. It is one of the most consistently replicated loci in psychiatric genetics. Each copy of the A allele at rs1006737 is associated on average with higher odds of bipolar disorder: a very small to small shift. Smaller associations are also reported for depression and schizophrenia. Bipolar disorder is highly polygenic, so this single variant shifts probability only slightly.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, the most common genotype. Associated with slightly lower average odds of bipolar disorder at this locus compared with A carriers. Because thousands of variants and non-genetic factors contribute, this genotype provides no meaningful protection on its own.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A allele, carried by a large share of the population. Associated on average with higher odds of bipolar disorder relative to GG — a very small to small shift against a low baseline likelihood. This is one small factor among very many; the large majority of people with this genotype never experience bipolar disorder.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele. Associated on average with modestly higher odds of bipolar disorder versus GG in combined analyses: a small shift. This remains a small effect on an uncommon condition: it is one contributing factor among thousands, and most people with this genotype are never affected.

title: Bipolar · ANK3
summary: ANK3 makes ankyrin-G, which helps place ion channels where nerve cells fire. In a broad DNA study, the less common T copy at rs10994336 was linked to higher odds of bipolar disorder. The odds ratio was about 1.45 in the first analysis and smaller in later groups. Like other common psychiatric markers, this change explains very little of the overall likelihood.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the common C allele. Associated with typical, slightly lower average odds of bipolar disorder at this locus. Overall likelihood still depends on thousands of other variants, family history, and life factors this report cannot see.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele, carried by roughly one in five people of European ancestry. Associated on average with moderately increased odds of bipolar disorder in genome-wide studies — a shift measured against a low population baseline. This is one small factor among very many, and the large majority of carriers are never affected.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies form an uncommon type. They mark the higher end of this DNA site's small link to bipolar disorder odds. The absolute likelihood still stays low for most people. This one change cannot show whether a person will be affected.

title: Schizophrenia · ZNF804A
summary: ZNF804A was among the first DNA regions to pass the broad study threshold for schizophrenia. The A copy at rs1344706 is called T in papers that use the other DNA strand. It is linked to higher odds of schizophrenia, a very small shift, against a lifetime baseline near 1%. Thousands of DNA and life factors are involved, so this marker says little about one person.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies mark the common risk form; some papers call it T because they use the other DNA strand. This type is linked to higher odds of schizophrenia versus CC: a small shift. Against the low baseline, the absolute shift is well under one percentage point. It is one tiny factor, and most people with AA are never affected.
interpretations.AC: One A and one C allele. Associated on average with higher odds of schizophrenia relative to CC, a very small statistical shift. This locus explains almost none of the person-to-person variation in likelihood, which depends on many genes and non-genetic factors.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele. Associated with slightly lower average odds of schizophrenia at this locus. Given how small the effect is and how many other factors contribute, this genotype is not meaningfully protective on its own.

title: Depression · OLFM4
summary: Depression is shaped by many genes. A study of more than 800,000 people found 102 separate DNA signals, each with a tiny effect. rs12552 near OLFM4 was among the strongest. Each A copy was linked to slightly higher odds of depression: a very small shift. No single change, including this one, can describe one person’s mood or outlook.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies are linked to higher odds of depression versus GG on average: a very small shift. The effect is so small that studies need hundreds of thousands of people to detect it. Depression reflects thousands of DNA changes and life events. This type alone says almost nothing about one person.
interpretations.AG: One A copy is linked to slightly higher odds of depression versus GG on average: a very small shift. This is one of the smallest effects in the app. It is a repeated population signal but carries almost no information about one person.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies are linked to marginally lower odds of depression at this site. More than 100 known signals each add very little, so this type is not protective in practice. Mood is shaped mostly by life context and many other genes.

title: Emotional reactivity · TPH2
summary: TPH2 controls the rate-limiting step of serotonin synthesis in the brain. In small brain-imaging studies, carriers of the T allele at the promoter variant rs4570625 (-703 G/T) showed, on average, stronger amygdala responses to emotional faces. Findings on anxiety and mood outcomes are mixed, and sample sizes have been small, so this association is preliminary.

interpretations.GG: Two G copies form the most common type. Small brain-scan studies link it to lower amygdala response to emotional images on average. Such lab results have only a loose link to daily emotional life. This change explains, at most, a tiny part of the differences between people.
interpretations.GT: One G and one T copy were included in the T-carrier group in small brain-scan studies. On average, that group showed a somewhat stronger amygdala response to emotional faces than GG. Study groups were modest and later results were mixed. This is a research clue, not a trait score.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies form an uncommon type. Small studies link T carriers to a stronger amygdala response to emotional images on average. Some researchers view this as greater emotional sensitivity. Links to anxiety or mood are not stable, so this remains one small, uncertain factor.

title: Research on BDNF and stress has mixed results.
summary: An older review linked the Met form of BDNF to depression after life stress. A much larger later study did not confirm this link. The difference matters: a finding about how a protein works does not establish how you cope with stress.

interpretations.CC: Your file shows two C copies, which code for Val. This was the comparison group for Met carriers in the older stress review. The later study did not confirm a mood-risk difference at this site. CC does not establish greater resilience or freedom from depression.
interpretations.CT: Your file shows one T copy, which codes for Met. The older review grouped people with one or two Met copies together. It found a link with depression after life stress, but the larger later study did not confirm it. This is not a personal stress score.
interpretations.TT: Your file shows two T copies, which code for Met. The older review pooled one-copy and two-copy Met carriers. It did not establish that TT has a stronger effect than CT. The larger later study did not confirm the stress link, so TT does not mean poor resilience.
